description: From Saxon shield walls and Viking raids to cavalry charges, longbows and linear tactics.
content_html:
How Battles Were Fought in the Early Medieval Period

Before the Norman Conquest of 1066, the armies of Britain were dominated by the infantry tactics of the Anglo-Saxons and the mobile raiding style of the Vikings. Understanding how these methods worked — and why they changed — is essential for tracing how British tactics evolved over more than a thousand years.

Saxon and Viking Battle Methods

The Anglo-Saxon army was built around the shield wall. Warriors — called huscarls (professional household troops) and fyrd (part-time levies) — locked their shields together to create a solid defensive line. This formation required strong discipline and worked best on firm ground where the line could hold. The shield wall was effective against cavalry charges but vulnerable if broken from the flanks or if discipline collapsed.

Viking armies used a similar shield wall when fighting pitched battles, but their strategic approach was fundamentally different. The Vikings were primarily raiders. Their use of longships allowed them to strike coastal and river targets rapidly, plunder and withdraw before a defensive force could be mustered. This hit-and-run raiding made conventional defensive responses difficult and forced Saxon England into a series of fortification programmes, including the system of burhs (fortified towns) developed under King Alfred of Wessex in the 880s.

Key Fact

The shield wall was the core infantry formation of both Anglo-Saxon and Viking warriors. Saxon armies used it defensively in pitched battle; Vikings used a similar formation when they chose to fight but preferred raiding over set-piece combat. The shield wall remained effective until cavalry tactics or missile weapons could break the line.

The Battle of Hastings, 1066

The Battle of Hastings on 14 October 1066 is one of the most important tactical engagements in British military history. Harold II’s Saxon army took up a strong defensive position on Senlac Hill and formed a shield wall. For much of the day, the Norman infantry and cavalry failed to break through. The Normans then used a tactical innovation: a feigned retreat that drew part of the Saxon line off the hill in pursuit. When the Normans turned to fight again, the broken Saxon formation was destroyed. William’s mounted knights delivered the decisive blow.

Hastings demonstrated the power of combined arms — coordinating archers, infantry and cavalry — against a force relying on a single tactic. It marked the beginning of the end for the old Saxon infantry-based method and introduced Norman cavalry dominance to Britain.

From the Conquest onwards, the mounted armoured knight became the dominant military figure in England. Knights were expensive to equip and maintain, and their social status — the feudal ideal of chivalry — was intertwined with their military role. In open-field battles, a cavalry charge by armoured knights could shatter an infantry line that lacked defensive preparation. However, this superiority was not absolute: cavalry charges struggled against disciplined pikemen, prepared defensive terrain and, most significantly, the English longbow.

The Longbow and the Battle of Crécy, 1346

The Battle of Crécy in August 1346 transformed medieval warfare. An English army under Edward III, with around 10,000 men, faced a larger French force that included armoured cavalry. The English deployed their longbowmen in massed formations on the flanks. As the French cavalry charged repeatedly, English volleys of arrows brought horses and riders down in large numbers. The disciplined firepower of the longbow shattered the tactical assumption that armoured cavalry was invincible.

Crécy was followed by similar English victories at Poitiers (1356) and Agincourt (1415). These battles demonstrated a key tactical principle: missile weapons, properly deployed with disciplined infantry support, could defeat the most prestigious heavy cavalry. The longbow required years of training to use effectively, which is why English and Welsh archers were genuinely feared across Europe.

Key Fact

The Battle of Crécy (1346) showed that disciplined longbow fire could defeat French armoured cavalry. English victories at Crécy, Poitiers (1356) and Agincourt (1415) all relied on this combination of missile weapons and defensive positioning, cementing the longbow as England’s signature weapon of the Hundred Years’ War.

Linear Tactics and the New Model Army

From the sixteenth century, the introduction of firearms gradually displaced the longbow and changed tactical formations. Linear tactics involved deploying musketeers in lines so that they could fire in sequence — one rank shooting while others reloaded — maintaining a near-continuous rate of fire. This required intensive drill and strict discipline.

The New Model Army, created by Parliament in 1645 during the English Civil War, represented a significant professionalisation of English military organisation. Unlike the feudal levies or ad hoc forces of earlier eras, it was a standing paid army with a clear command structure, uniform training and a regimental system. Its victories at Naseby (June 1645) and Langport (July 1645) effectively ended the first phase of the Civil War. The New Model Army’s model — professional, trained, disciplined — pointed towards the kind of armies that would dominate British warfare into the nineteenth century.

Across the medieval and early modern periods, several elements changed significantly: the dominant arm shifted from infantry (shield wall) to cavalry (Norman knight) to missile (longbow) to firearm (musket and then rifle). However, one continuous factor was the importance of discipline. Whether holding a shield wall, maintaining arrow volleys at Crécy, or firing in linear sequence, disciplined soldiers consistently outperformed undisciplined ones. This continuity — the premium placed on training and formation — runs through the entire history of British land warfare up to the mid nineteenth century.
exam_tip_html: For 8-mark ‘Explain Change’ questions about tactics, you need to describe what changed and why it changed. Don’t just say the longbow replaced cavalry — explain what made it so effective (rate of fire, range, ability to penetrate armour from a distance) and link it to a specific battle as evidence. For 16-mark thematic essays, use the tactical shifts covered here as your medieval and early modern evidence, then connect them to the modern period (trenches, combined arms, asymmetric warfare) in later lessons.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Saxon and Viking armies relied on the shield wall; the Norman Conquest (1066) introduced cavalry dominance to Britain and demonstrated the value of combined arms at Hastings.
  • The Battle of Crécy (1346) showed that disciplined longbow fire could defeat armoured cavalry, making the longbow England’s signature weapon for the next century.
  • The New Model Army (1645) professionalised English land forces and established linear tactics with firearms; discipline remained the constant factor across all tactical eras.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Saxon shield wall as a battle tactic.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks. Students should identify a feature and support it:
• The shield wall involved warriors locking their shields together to form a continuous defensive line [1], making it very difficult for attacking infantry or cavalry to break through without disrupting the formation [1].
• Professional huscarls formed the core of the shield wall, providing the discipline needed to hold the formation [1+1].

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the New Model Army created in 1645.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail):
• Feature 1: It was a professional, paid standing army [1], unlike the feudal levies that preceded it, which ensured consistent training and discipline [1].
• Feature 2: It had a clear command structure and uniform regimental system [1], which allowed coordinated manoeuvres and contributed to decisive victories at Naseby and Langport in 1645 [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why the Battle of Hastings (1066) was significant for the development of medieval tactics.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains the significance in depth — the Norman use of combined arms (archers, infantry, cavalry) and the feigned retreat broke the Saxon shield wall and demonstrated the vulnerability of infantry-only formations to disciplined cavalry. Analyses the longer-term consequence: Norman cavalry dominance replaced Saxon infantry as the core of English armies.
Secure: Clear explanation with relevant supporting evidence.
Developing: Identifies significance with limited development.
Emerging: Simple statement with little evidence.

practice_questions.text: Explain the change in English tactics between c.1000 and c.1500.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Traces change from Saxon shield wall → Norman cavalry → longbow tactics (Crécy 1346, Agincourt 1415). Explains the reasons for each shift and weighs which was most significant. Reaches a substantiated conclusion.
Secure: Covers at least two tactical changes with relevant evidence and an explanation of cause.
Developing: Describes changes but analysis is limited.
Emerging: Simple description of one tactic; no analysis of change.

practice_questions.text: How significant was the longbow in changing English tactics in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries? Use specific evidence to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Argues significance at the time (Crécy 1346, Poitiers 1356, Agincourt 1415 — all decisive English victories against larger forces) and over time (established the principle that missile power and discipline can defeat armoured shock troops; influenced subsequent firearms development). Concludes on degree of significance.
Secure: Explains significance with battle evidence and some analysis.
Developing: Identifies battles but analysis is thin.
Emerging: Describes the longbow without evaluating its significance.

practice_questions.text: How far did tactics change in Britain between c.500 and the mid nineteenth century? In your answer, cover at least two eras.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Traces change across medieval (shield wall → cavalry → longbow) and early modern (firearms → linear tactics → New Model Army) eras. Identifies continuity (discipline as constant; combined arms as recurring theme). Weighs change against continuity and reaches a substantiated overall judgement on how far and why tactics changed.
Secure: Covers both eras with evidence, some analysis of change/continuity, and a conclusion.
Developing: Covers one era well; limited analysis.
Emerging: Describes events without analysing change.

glossary_terms.definition: A defensive formation in which warriors stand shoulder to shoulder with overlapping shields, presenting a continuous wall to the enemy.
A military strategy based on swift, surprise attacks with small mobile forces rather than pitched set-piece battles.
Heavy cavalry that formed the elite striking force of Norman armies, trained to charge and break enemy formations.
Archers using a weapon up to 1.8 metres long, made from yew, capable of firing arrows at high speed and long range, used to devastating effect by English armies in the Hundred Years' War.
A battlefield formation in which soldiers are arranged in long rows, allowing them to fire in coordinated volleys and reload while others fire.
The professional parliamentary army created in 1645 during the English Civil War, noted for its discipline, training and religious motivation.
